title: Attention as a shape and information-flow contract
summary: Q, K and V have different roles; the mask defines what information is allowed to flow.
explanation: For Q∈R^(Tq×d), K∈R^(Tk×d), V∈R^(Tk×dv), the score matrix is Tq×Tk and the result is Tq×dv. Normalize over keys. A causal mask belongs before normalization, and a padded query may need its output discarded separately. Shape agreement alone cannot establish correct masking.
example: With two zero-score queries and values [2,6], causal outputs are [2,4]. Replacing the second value by 100 must leave the first output at 2.
pitfalls: Masking after softmax without renormalization changes row sums.
A fully masked row can produce NaNs.
A transposed softmax axis can silently pass shape tests.

question.prompt: Design tests for causal attention that do more than check the output shape.
question.answer: Check a hand-computed example, finite row sums, and invariance of earlier outputs to future-token changes. Test unequal query and key lengths explicitly; an offset-aware decode mask differs from a square training mask. Compare against an independent implementation on seeded random inputs.
followups: Which test detects a mask with the wrong offset during cached decoding?
How would you handle a query with no valid key?
rubric: Identify Q/K/V and score/output dimensions.
Normalize over keys and apply masks before softmax.
Test future-token invariance and fully masked rows.
Compare with an independent implementation and a stated tolerance.

title: Grouped-query attention and cache pressure
summary: Query heads and key/value heads need not have the same count.
explanation: Multi-head attention gives each query head its own K/V head. Multi-query attention shares one; grouped-query attention shares one K/V head across a group of query heads. This changes cache size, not the number of query heads. Compare quality, bandwidth, and checkpoint compatibility rather than assuming fewer heads always wins.
example: For B=1, L=32, T=4096, Hkv=8, dh=128, and b=2 bytes, the cache is 536,870,912 bytes: 512 MiB. Using 32 K/V heads multiplies that by four.
pitfalls: Confusing query-head count with K/V-head count.
Ignoring batch and layer factors.
Treating a checkpoint conversion as a reshape.

question.prompt: Estimate the KV memory saved by reducing 32 K/V heads to 8. What could you lose?
question.answer: The K/V cache falls by a factor of four at fixed dimensions, sequence length, batch and dtype. Discuss reduced representational freedom, conversion/uptraining, and the need to validate quality. End-to-end latency also depends on kernel support and the serving workload.
followups: Why does this help decode more than prefill?
What must be checked before grouping existing checkpoint heads?
rubric: Distinguish query heads from shared K/V heads.
Include batch, layers, length, head dimension and dtype in cache bytes.
Calculate the fourfold cache reduction in the example.
Explain checkpoint conversion and quality/kernel tradeoffs.

title: Rotary positions and cached decoding
summary: Position transforms must stay consistent when generation uses a cache.
explanation: RoPE applies position-dependent rotations to paired query and key coordinates. Their inner product encodes relative-position structure. During cached generation, new queries and keys use their absolute sequence positions; restarting positions at zero changes the computation. Longer-context modifications need explicit evaluation rather than an extrapolation guarantee.
example: If a prompt fills positions 0 through 127, the next token uses position 128 even though its query tensor has sequence length one. Compare cached and full-prefix logits at every step.
pitfalls: Rotating cached keys twice.
Resetting positions for each decode step.
Assuming arbitrary context extension preserves quality.

question.prompt: How would you debug a model whose cached and uncached generation disagree?
question.answer: Disable stochastic layers, fix token inputs, and compare logits step by step. Check position indices, cache offsets, key rotation, mask alignment, dtype and layout. Use short sequences first and tolerances appropriate to the computation.
followups: What changes if cache entries are evicted?
Why might token outputs differ even for close logits?
rubric: Use the absolute cache position for each new token.
Explain the relative-position effect of paired rotations.
Avoid rotating stored keys a second time.
Compare cached and full-prefix logits at matching positions and tolerance.

title: FlashAttention: arithmetic versus memory traffic
summary: An exact attention implementation can be faster without making attention sparse.
explanation: FlashAttention organizes attention around GPU memory traffic and tiled computation. It avoids materializing the full attention matrix in high-bandwidth memory. Online normalization combines blocks while preserving the mathematical softmax result, up to floating-point differences. Dense attention still has quadratic interactions; lower memory traffic is not the same as linear-time attention.
example: A 4096×4096 score matrix contains 16,777,216 elements. At two bytes each that is 32 MiB per head before accounting for other intermediates. Avoiding that write/read can matter even when arithmetic is unchanged.
pitfalls: Calling it approximate attention.
Equating memory savings with linear arithmetic.
Benchmarking only one sequence length.

question.prompt: Explain how exact attention can use less memory and run faster.
question.answer: Distinguish arithmetic, memory footprint and memory traffic. Describe tiling and online softmax statistics. Discuss recomputation and hardware-dependent performance; validate output and gradient tolerances before reporting speedups.
followups: When might a small attention kernel fail to benefit?
How should a benchmark separate warmup and compilation?
rubric: Explain tiled online softmax and avoided materialized scores.
Distinguish quadratic arithmetic from reduced memory traffic.
State numerical tolerances rather than bitwise identity.
Benchmark representative shapes with warmup and GPU synchronization.

title: KV cache accounting and equivalence tests
summary: A cache trades persistent memory for avoiding repeated key/value computation.
explanation: A decoder stores each layer’s keys and values for earlier tokens. Prefill processes a prompt; decode adds tokens while reusing that state. Cache size grows with retained tokens and active sequences. Correctness requires position offsets, sequence ownership, causal masking and eviction policy to agree with the intended model.
equation: bytes=2\times B\times L\times T\times H_{KV}\times d_h\times bytes_{element}
example: A two-token prefix followed by a one-token append should produce the same last-token output as a full three-token forward pass when stochasticity is disabled. Test two sequences whose cache slots are interleaved to detect cross-request leakage.
pitfalls: Forgetting the factor of two for keys and values.
Reusing one request’s slots for another.
Comparing sampled tokens instead of logits.

question.prompt: Design a cache API and its most important correctness tests.
question.answer: Specify append, read, reset, capacity and ownership. Test cached/full equivalence, nonzero offsets, independent sequences, and the boundary at capacity. Explain whether eviction changes context semantics. A reset must clear length and ownership even if storage is reused.
followups: How does beam branching affect sharing?
What changes for sliding-window attention?
rubric: Account for both keys and values across all layers.
State dtype, batch and K/V head assumptions.
Compare cached and full-prefix logits before sampling.
Test offsets, capacity and request isolation.

title: Continuous batching and latency budgets
summary: Serving is a scheduling problem with variable sequence lengths.
explanation: Continuous batching admits and retires requests as generation proceeds. Throughput, time to first token, time per output token, fairness and memory occupancy are different objectives. Long prefills can delay decode work unless scheduling bounds interference. Backpressure must be defined before the queue becomes unbounded.
example: Two services can both emit 1000 tokens/s while one keeps a user waiting 8 seconds before the first token. Report latency percentiles and arrival patterns alongside aggregate throughput.
pitfalls: Optimizing tokens/s while ignoring queue latency.
Comparing different output-length distributions.
No policy for canceled requests.

question.prompt: Design admission control for a bursty LLM endpoint.
question.answer: Clarify latency SLOs and workload distribution. Bound queues, reserve memory for output growth, and define reject/degrade behavior. Measure prefill/decode interference, fairness, cancellation cleanup and tail latency under open-loop load.
followups: Would you prioritize short requests?
How would you prevent long-request starvation?
rubric: Distinguish prefill from decode workloads.
Include queueing time in the latency budget.
Handle cancellation and release cache ownership.
Compare tail latency and throughput under identical request distributions.

title: Paged KV storage and fragmentation
summary: Logical token positions need not occupy one contiguous physical allocation.
explanation: PagedAttention uses block-based KV storage with a mapping from logical blocks to physical blocks. This can reduce fragmentation and support sharing of common prefixes. Indirection and block size introduce their own costs. A memory allocator and an attention kernel must agree on ownership, layout and valid lengths.
example: With block size 16 and a 17-token sequence, two blocks hold 32 token slots; 15 slots are unused in the last block. Smaller blocks reduce tail waste but increase metadata and mapping work.
pitfalls: Claiming paging removes all memory overhead.
Ignoring reference counts for shared blocks.
Reading unwritten slots in the tail block.

question.prompt: What invariants would you test in a paged KV allocator?
question.answer: No block may be simultaneously writable by unrelated sequences. Shared immutable prefixes need safe reference counting or copy-on-write. Free only after the final owner releases a block. Check valid token bounds and recovery after cancellation.
followups: How would you test allocator churn?
What happens when two requests diverge after a shared prefix?
rubric: Separate logical positions from physical cache blocks.
Calculate block utilization and tail waste.
Track shared-block ownership and reference counts.
Test release, reuse and partial-block reads.

title: Speculative decoding and distribution preservation
summary: A faster draft model proposes work; the target model validates it.
explanation: Speculative decoding can verify several draft tokens in one target pass. Exact sampling schemes include acceptance and correction rules so the resulting distribution matches the target’s. Greedy agreement alone is not a proof for stochastic sampling. Benefit depends on acceptance rate, draft cost, verification cost and hardware utilization.
equation: speedup\approx\frac{accepted\ tokens\ per\ cycle}{relative\ cycle\ cost}
example: If a cycle yields three accepted output tokens but costs the equivalent of two ordinary target steps, the toy speedup is 1.5×. Include rejected proposals and draft overhead when measuring actual service throughput.
pitfalls: Assuming draft accuracy alone predicts speedup.
Dropping the correction distribution.
Comparing different sampling settings.

question.prompt: When can speculative decoding make inference slower?
question.answer: A costly draft, low acceptance, or expensive verification can erase gains. Benchmark matched prompts and sampling parameters, include both models’ work, and measure end-to-end latency rather than accepted-token rate alone.
followups: How would you validate the output distribution?
Why does batch size change the tradeoff?
rubric: State draft and target distributions and support assumptions.
Explain acceptance and the residual correction distribution.
Distinguish distribution preservation from a greedy shortcut.
Measure draft overhead and accepted tokens per target step.

title: Compute budgets and scaling decisions
summary: Model size, token count and training budget are coupled choices.
explanation: Compute-optimal scaling studies allocate a fixed training budget between model parameters and data. Their fitted optima depend on model family, data and the measured regime. A training-optimal choice may differ from a deployment-optimal one when inference volume, latency or memory dominates lifetime cost.
example: At N=1 billion parameters and D=20 billion tokens, 6ND is 1.2×10²⁰ FLOPs. This estimate omits important architecture and utilization details; it is a sizing tool, not a wall-time measurement.
pitfalls: Treating an empirical scaling fit as a universal law.
Using peak GPU FLOPs as achieved throughput.
Ignoring data quality and repeated data.

question.prompt: How would you choose between a larger undertrained model and a smaller longer-trained one?
question.answer: State the fixed budget and deployment constraints. Compare validation quality and downstream evaluation at matched compute, include data availability, then model expected inference cost. Explain which result would change the decision.
followups: How does high inference volume change the objective?
What evidence would show data quality is the bottleneck?
rubric: State whether training or inference FLOPs are being estimated.
Include token count, parameters and useful utilization assumptions.
Separate peak hardware rate from measured throughput.
Control data quality and total budget when comparing scaling choices.

title: AdamW and decoupled regularization
summary: Adaptive gradient scaling changes how L2 penalties behave.
explanation: Adding an L2 penalty to the loss sends its gradient through the optimizer’s adaptive scaling. Decoupled weight decay applies a separate parameter shrinkage step. With adaptive optimizers these are generally different updates. Report which parameter groups receive decay; biases and normalization parameters may follow a deliberate separate policy.
example: With zero gradient, learning rate 0.1, weight decay 0.2 and weight 5, the decoupled shrinkage alone gives 4.9. This isolates decay behavior from momentum and gradient normalization.
pitfalls: Equating Adam plus L2 with AdamW.
Applying decay twice.
Comparing runs with different effective learning rates.

question.prompt: Why does decoupled weight decay differ from adding an L2 loss term under Adam?
question.answer: The loss penalty contributes to the gradient moments and is rescaled coordinate-wise. Decoupled decay shrinks the parameters separately. Write both updates, explain the distinction, and use a zero-gradient test to isolate shrinkage.
followups: Should every parameter receive decay?
How do you checkpoint optimizer state correctly?
rubric: Distinguish decoupled decay from an L2 gradient term.
Update first/second moments and bias corrections correctly.
Apply decay once with the intended learning rate.
Check the update against a small independent numeric example.

title: Gradient accumulation without changing the objective
summary: Microbatching only reproduces a large-batch update when weighting and update boundaries match.
explanation: Accumulate gradients across microbatches, then update once. Equal-size microbatches can average losses uniformly; unequal token counts require token-weighted normalization for a token-average objective. Clipping, scheduling, zeroing and mixed-precision unscaling must happen at the intended optimizer-step boundary.
example: Microbatches with 2 and 6 valid tokens have mean gradients 1 and 3. The correct token-average gradient is (2×1+6×3)/8=2.5, not the unweighted mean 2.
pitfalls: Dividing by accumulation steps when microbatches have unequal weight.
Clipping each microbatch separately.
Advancing the scheduler on every microbatch.

question.prompt: Why might accumulated training differ from a single large batch?
question.answer: Check loss weighting, stochastic layers, batch-dependent normalization, floating-point order and optimizer-step frequency. Compare gradients before the update on a tiny deterministic example, then isolate one source of divergence at a time.
followups: What if the final accumulation window is shorter?
How do variable-length sequences affect normalization?
rubric: Normalize by valid target tokens across the entire update.
Handle unequal microbatch token counts.
Clip and advance the optimizer/scheduler at update boundaries.
Compare accumulated gradients with a full-batch baseline.

title: Mixed precision and numerical diagnosis
summary: Storage dtype, compute dtype and accumulation dtype are separate decisions.
explanation: Reduced-precision computation can improve throughput and memory use, but different formats have different exponent ranges and precision. Loss scaling protects small gradients in some workflows; it does not repair an unstable forward expression. Inspect where the first nonfinite value appears and maintain sensitive reductions in an appropriate dtype.
example: A NaN may originate in a fully masked attention row before backward begins. Increasing a gradient scale cannot repair it. Log the first failing layer and test the same tiny batch in higher precision.
pitfalls: Treating all 16-bit formats as interchangeable.
Clipping scaled gradients before unscaling.
Assuming loss scaling fixes forward overflow.

question.prompt: A training run becomes NaN only in mixed precision. What do you inspect?
question.answer: Reproduce on one batch; find the earliest nonfinite activation, loss or gradient. Check mask rows, exponentials, division denominators, scaling/unscaling order, and optimizer state. Compare selected operations in higher precision rather than changing everything at once.
followups: How do you distinguish underflow from overflow?
What should a skipped optimizer step do to a scheduler?
rubric: Distinguish BF16 exponent range from FP16 precision/range.
Locate the first nonfinite intermediate.
Unscale FP16 gradients before clipping when scaling is used.
Compare a suspect operation against an FP32 reference.

title: LoRA: parameter efficiency is not universal memory efficiency
summary: A low-rank update reduces trainable parameters but leaves other memory costs.
explanation: LoRA represents a weight update through low-rank factors while freezing the base weight. Trainable parameter count drops from dout×din to r(dout+din) per adapted matrix. Activations, base weights and optimizer choices still affect memory. Adapter rank and target modules are modeling decisions that should be evaluated.
equation: \Delta W=BA,\quad A\in\mathbb R^{r\times d_{in}},B\in\mathbb R^{d_{out}\times r}
example: For a 4096×4096 matrix and rank 8, factors contain 65,536 parameters versus 16,777,216 in the full matrix. That is a parameter-count comparison, not a claim of 256× total GPU memory savings.
pitfalls: Ignoring activation memory.
Failing to apply the intended adapter scaling.
Assuming the same rank suits every layer and task.

question.prompt: How would you evaluate an adapter configuration under a fixed memory budget?
question.answer: Measure peak memory and quality under matched data, tokens, precision and batch settings. Sweep rank and target modules, account for base-model storage, and compare trainable-state savings separately from activation costs.
followups: When can merging adapters help serving?
What evidence suggests the rank is too restrictive?
rubric: State dimensions and rank of the two adapter factors.
Apply alpha/r scaling once.
Separate trainable parameter savings from activation memory.
Validate adapter-enabled and merged behavior under a fixed base revision.

title: Supervised fine-tuning as a data and loss contract
summary: A valid text example is not automatically a valid supervised objective.
explanation: Specify which tokens contribute to the loss and which tokens are context. Preserve conversation boundaries, role formatting and train/evaluation separation. Inspect actual tokenized examples and masks rather than trusting a preprocessing pipeline. Repeated templates, leakage and mislabeled targets can dominate the apparent gain.
example: If a 100-token conversation has 20 answer tokens, a response-only loss has 20 targets. Counting all 100 tokens changes the objective and loss normalization. Check a decoded example with target positions highlighted.
pitfalls: Training on prompt tokens unintentionally.
Leaking held-out prompts through near duplicates.
Comparing losses with different masking conventions.

question.prompt: What checks would you run before an expensive fine-tune?
question.answer: Inspect tokenization, truncation, role boundaries, loss masks and target counts. Overfit a tiny clean batch, verify held-out deduplication, and establish a base-model evaluation. Log exact data and preprocessing versions.
followups: How would you handle packed conversations?
What can a lower training loss fail to tell you?
rubric: Show exact tokenizer-aligned supervised target positions.
Preserve the model chat template and avoid double-shifting labels.
Reject examples with zero retained causal targets.
Keep source groups and near-duplicates out of held-out splits.

title: DPO: reference-relative preference learning
summary: Preference optimization depends on the reference and the data distribution.
explanation: DPO trains on preferred and dispreferred responses using policy/reference log-probability differences. It avoids an explicit reward-model optimization loop in its basic formulation, but it does not remove preference-label quality or distribution-shift concerns. The reference model and temperature-like scaling influence the update.
example: A preferred response can improve relative to a rejected one while both remain poor by an external rubric. Evaluate absolute task quality and safety separately from pairwise training accuracy.
pitfalls: Omitting the reference terms.
Confusing preference accuracy with general alignment.
Not checking response-length confounds.

question.prompt: What would you investigate if DPO improves pairwise accuracy but hurts task success?
question.answer: Audit preference construction, response lengths, domain shift and reference choice. Compare absolute task metrics and stratified failure cases. Run controlled data ablations before attributing the change to the objective itself.
followups: How would you detect a labeling shortcut?
What role does the reference play?
rubric: Use both policy and frozen-reference sequence log-probabilities.
Compute the chosen/rejected reference-relative margin.
Evaluate log-sigmoid stably at extreme margins.
Discuss beta, response length and held-out preference validity.

title: Preference labels, reward proxies and held-out evidence
summary: A preference label is a measurement with assumptions and noise.
explanation: Write a rubric before collecting comparisons. A judge may favor verbosity, style, position or familiarity rather than correctness. Hold out prompts and evaluate with independent criteria. Optimizing a proxy can amplify its blind spots; a better proxy score alone is not enough evidence of a better system.
example: Create a pair where one response is longer but contains a subtle factual error. Reverse response order and compare judge decisions. This probes two biases without pretending to establish every judge failure mode.
pitfalls: Reusing training judges as the only evaluator.
Ignoring disagreement between annotators.
Treating a proxy as the intended objective.

question.prompt: How do you test whether a preference dataset rewards verbosity instead of correctness?
question.answer: Construct matched-length and length-controlled pairs, stratify by length difference, randomize position, and compare to an independent correctness rubric. Review disagreements manually and repeat after training.
followups: How would you quantify label uncertainty?
What data ablation would be informative?
rubric: Specify what annotators compare and under which instructions.
Record disagreement and source-group provenance.
Test response length and style as possible confounds.
Use an evaluator independent of the training reward proxy.

title: Paired evaluation and uncertainty
summary: Evaluate the difference on the same examples rather than comparing two isolated percentages.
explanation: Use a held-out task set and record per-example outcomes for both systems. Paired analysis preserves shared example difficulty. Resampling should respect the unit of independence: related questions, users or documents may need cluster-level sampling. Confidence intervals describe uncertainty under a sampling model, not immunity to bias or leakage.
example: A new model changes 12 of 100 examples: eight become correct and four become wrong. The net improvement is four points, but the pattern of changed outcomes is more informative than two aggregate accuracies.
pitfalls: Treating correlated examples as independent.
Testing repeatedly on the same holdout.
Reporting only the best seed.

question.prompt: A benchmark rises from 72% to 74%. Is the change meaningful?
question.answer: Ask for sample size, paired outcomes, sampling unit, seeds and the decision threshold. Compute an appropriate uncertainty interval and inspect regressions. Separate statistical uncertainty from contamination and benchmark relevance.
followups: What if examples share one source document?
How would repeated experimentation affect confidence?
rubric: Align both models on the same task IDs.
Count wins, losses and ties with the correct denominator.
Resample paired tasks or source groups for uncertainty.
Report regressions and repeated-test/selection limitations.

title: Benchmark scores, contamination and task validity
summary: A score only supports claims about the measured distribution and evaluation protocol.
explanation: Define the capability and failure costs before selecting a benchmark. Track dataset versions, prompts, model settings, scoring rules and exclusion criteria. Near duplicates and public test exposure can invalidate a clean generalization story. Use fresh task slices and error analysis to complement a headline score.
example: A code generator may pass visible tests yet fail on input mutation, timeout, or an untested edge case. Add independent adversarial cases and state what the test suite does not measure.
pitfalls: Equating test-set success with deployment reliability.
Changing prompts between model comparisons.
Calling public benchmark exposure proof of memorization.

question.prompt: Design an evaluation for an internal code assistant.
question.answer: Sample actual tasks with permissions and privacy controls, reserve held-out repositories or time periods, define correctness and latency criteria, and add human-reviewed failure categories. Log versions and evaluate security-relevant failures separately.
followups: How do you prevent leakage between repository splits?
When is execution success an inadequate metric?
rubric: Define the actual task and deployment population.
Distinguish exposure, overlap and proven memorization.
Keep prompt, decoding and budget fixed across comparisons.
Protect an untouched holdout and report slice-specific failures.

title: Separate retrieval failures from generation failures
summary: End-to-end answers hide which stage failed.
explanation: Evaluate retrieval against relevant evidence, then evaluate generation conditional on the available evidence. Include an oracle-context condition and a no-context baseline. Citation presence does not establish support; verify that cited passages actually entail the answer. Retrieval quality and access control must both hold.
example: If oracle context fixes a task but normal retrieval does not, investigate chunking, query construction and ranking. If the model still fails with the answer passage supplied, retrieval tuning alone is unlikely to fix it.
pitfalls: Scoring citations without checking support.
Retrieving documents the user cannot access.
Testing only answerable questions.

question.prompt: How would you debug a RAG system with plausible but unsupported answers?
question.answer: Inspect retrieved evidence and permissions, add oracle-context and unanswerable conditions, score support independently, and distinguish missing evidence from failure to use evidence. Define abstention behavior and freshness requirements.
followups: How would you measure retrieval coverage?
What happens when relevant documents conflict?
rubric: Measure retrieval coverage before judging generation.
Verify cited passages support each answer claim.
Include unanswerable queries and permission restrictions.
Separate wrong evidence from unsupported use of correct evidence.

title: Reproduction, ablation and falsifiable claims
summary: A reproduction needs an experiment contract, not only a random seed.
explanation: Record code, data splits, preprocessing, dependencies, hardware, precision, initialization and checkpoint state. Distinguish reproducing a published procedure from independently confirming its conclusion. An ablation changes a specific factor while keeping meaningful controls matched. Report negative results and uncertainty rather than selecting one favorable run.
example: To test a normalization change, keep data order, training budget and evaluation fixed. Compare several seeds and inspect whether the apparent gain is smaller than ordinary run-to-run variation.
pitfalls: Assuming a seed guarantees cross-device identity.
Changing multiple factors in an ablation.
Omitting optimizer and sampler state on resume.

question.prompt: What belongs in a reproducibility package for a training result?
question.answer: Include executable configuration, exact dataset/split provenance, environment lockfiles, seed policy, evaluation procedure, logs and checkpoint/resume state. State known nondeterminism and distinguish qualitative replication from numerical identity.
followups: What would falsify the paper’s main claim?
How would you investigate a failed reproduction?
rubric: Pin source, data, model revision and dependency versions.
Restore optimizer, RNG and sampler state when resuming.
Change one factor in a controlled ablation.
State hardware/numerical limits and report all planned seeds.

title: Retrieval as a versioned evidence pipeline
summary: An embedding similarity score is not a guarantee of relevance, truth or permission.
explanation: Define the corpus, document versions, chunk boundaries, retrieval filters and reranking contract. Metadata such as tenant, timestamp and authority belongs in the retrieval design. Test whether the answer is recoverable from the returned passages, and retain provenance so errors can be traced to a specific corpus version.
example: A highly similar paragraph from another tenant is an incorrect result even if it answers the question. Test permission filters before evaluating semantic relevance, including empty-result cases.
pitfalls: Filtering permissions only after generation.
No deletion or freshness policy.
Choosing chunk size on one easy query.

question.prompt: Design a multi-tenant retrieval service.
question.answer: Authenticate the caller, enforce tenant and document permissions at retrieval, version the index, and define deletion/freshness behavior. Evaluate relevance, support, latency and isolation on adversarial cases. Explain failure behavior when retrieval is empty.
followups: How would you remove a document from cached answers?
When would hybrid retrieval help?
rubric: Version documents, chunks, embeddings and index configuration.
Enforce access before evidence reaches generation.
Define deletion, freshness and indexing behavior.
Evaluate ranked retrieval across representative query slices.

title: Tool execution, idempotency and trust boundaries
summary: A model-generated tool call is a proposed action, not an authorization decision.
explanation: Validate schema and permissions outside the model. Separate planning, approval where needed, execution and result interpretation. Side effects require idempotency keys or another retry policy; a network timeout does not prove an action failed. Treat returned documents and tool text as data that cannot grant new permissions.
equation: at\ least\ once\ delivery+idempotency\to controlled\ effects
example: If a payment-like operation times out after execution, retrying with a new identifier may duplicate the effect. Query status or retry with the same idempotency key according to the service contract.
pitfalls: Trusting retrieved text as an instruction.
Retrying non-idempotent effects blindly.
Only validating JSON syntax.

question.prompt: How do you make a tool-using agent safe to retry?
question.answer: Define action identity, authorization, validation, bounded retries, timeouts and reconciliation. Distinguish read-only actions from effects. Log enough state to determine whether an action completed without storing unnecessary sensitive payloads.
followups: What if a tool result asks for broader access?
How would you recover after the client disconnects?
rubric: Validate arguments and authorize effects outside the model.
Use stable operation keys across retries.
Reject conflicting key reuse and make ledger/effect updates atomic.
Test timeout-after-effect, replay and untrusted retrieved instructions.

title: Evaluate trajectories and recovery, not just final prose
summary: A plausible answer can hide a broken action sequence.
explanation: Instrument tool choices, arguments, state transitions, side effects and recovery. Score task completion separately from cost, latency and policy compliance. Use deterministic test environments where possible and introduce controlled failures. A final answer is only one observable artifact of an agent’s behavior.
example: Inject a timeout after a successful write, a stale document version and an empty search result. Check whether the agent reconciles state, refreshes evidence, or stops with an accurate explanation.
pitfalls: Scoring only fluent final responses.
Unbounded retry loops.
Evaluating on a different environment each run.

question.prompt: Create an evaluation plan for a multi-step research assistant.
question.answer: Specify tasks, evidence standards, allowed tools and resource budgets. Record trajectories, include injected failures and misleading retrieved text, and independently verify citations and side effects. Measure recovery and uncertainty reporting.
followups: How would you compare two agent policies fairly?
What is the unit of a successful task?
rubric: Score final environment state and intermediate actions.
Keep success, safety violations and budget consumption separate.
Freeze initial state and reset between trials.
Inject failures and report repeated-trial recovery behavior.

title: Data loaders, sharding and resumable experiments
summary: The sampler’s state is part of the training state.
explanation: Define whether each example is seen exactly once per epoch, how shards are assigned, and what happens to incomplete batches. Distributed ranks must agree on progress without duplicating or silently omitting data. Resume needs data order and sampler position as well as model and optimizer weights.
equation: global\ batch=microbatch\times accumulation\times data\ parallel\ ranks
example: For ten examples split across three ranks, decide explicitly whether to pad, drop or allow unequal shard sizes. Then test the union of rank assignments and their intersections under the stated contract.
pitfalls: Every rank using the same shuffle without disjoint slicing.
Saving weights but not sampler position.
Silent duplicates introduced to equalize batch counts.

question.prompt: Design a sharded data loader and its resume tests.
question.answer: Specify deterministic ordering, disjoint assignment, tail handling and checkpoint state. Test union coverage, rank intersections, epoch transitions and resume equivalence. State whether the contract permits padded duplicates.
followups: What if world size changes after resume?
How do worker prefetch queues affect exact replay?
rubric: Assign disjoint source samples to ranks/workers.
Specify shuffling and tail-batch behavior.
Checkpoint sampler cursor and random state with training state.
Verify no unintended gaps or duplicates after resume.

title: Tokenization, chat templates and causal loss boundaries
summary: Training labels must agree with the official tokenizer, rendered turns and the causal loss shift.
explanation: Render conversations with the model’s official tokenizer and chat template. Construct or obtain token-aligned assistant masks, preserve labels at the same positions as input IDs, and let the causal language-model loss shift logits and targets. Inspect EOS, padding, packing boundaries and truncation. A nonempty rendered conversation may still contain zero usable supervised targets. Fail before training if the label contract cannot be verified.
example: For tokens [10,11,12,13] with assistant targets at positions 2 and 3, labels are [-100,-100,12,13]. A limit of 2 removes every target and must fail. Do not pre-shift and then let the trainer shift again.
pitfalls: Guessing token boundaries with string delimiters.
Counting padding as a target.
Packing documents without checking boundary attention and loss.

sources.title: TRL SFT data and loss contracts

question.prompt: How would you prove an SFT job trains only on the intended assistant tokens?
question.answer: Inspect decoded input/label pairs from the official template, assert token-prefix or generation-mask alignment, and count usable shifted targets after truncation. Check padding and packed boundaries explicitly. Overfit a tiny verified set before a full run, and compare validation under the same masking convention.
followups: What counterexample would break your design?
What evidence would make you change this choice?
rubric: Use the official tokenizer/template.
Show exact supervised positions and the internal causal shift.
Reject zero-target truncations.
Test padding, EOS and packed sequence boundaries.

title: QLoRA, quantization error and deployment parity
summary: Quantized frozen weights, adapter parameters, compute dtype and KV cache are different memory terms.
explanation: QLoRA trains adapters through a quantized frozen base. Distinguish storage format from compute dtype and distinguish both from the precision of activations, optimizer state and KV cache. A uniform toy quantizer illustrates rounding error but does not implement NF4 or a deployment format. Merging or exporting changes the loading path; compare actual outputs and task metrics before asserting parity.
example: A uniform block [-2,0,2] with qmax=2 uses scale 1 and reconstructs exactly. A value halfway between codes exposes rounding conventions. Real quality checks need model-level held-out evaluation as well as scalar error.
pitfalls: Calling every 4-bit format interchangeable.
Assuming adapters eliminate activation memory.
Claiming an exported model is equivalent without testing it.

question.prompt: Why can a 4-bit fine-tune still run out of memory, and how would you validate an export?
question.answer: Frozen weight compression does not remove activations, adapters, optimizer state or the KV cache. Measure the peak under the actual context and batch. Load the original and exported artifacts under controlled decoding, compare numerical differences where appropriate, and repeat held-out task and performance evaluation. Record format and converter versions.
followups: What counterexample would break your design?
What evidence would make you change this choice?
rubric: Separate weight, activation, optimizer and cache memory.
State rounding/grouping and compute dtype assumptions.
Identify what merging/export changes.
Compare quality and resources under fixed decoding.

title: Context budgets, durable state and agent recovery
summary: Select relevant context while preserving explicit state and authority across interruptions.
explanation: Context engineering chooses what evidence, instructions and tool results fit in the active token window. Durable workflow state lives outside that window and records completed effects, pending work and artifact versions. Compaction should preserve decisions and unresolved questions without promoting retrieved text into authority. Budget for tool responses and generation, and evaluate task success after interruption rather than only testing short prompts.
example: A workflow completed operation A before disconnecting. Its next runtime should read a durable operation record, refresh stale evidence, and continue with B. Repeating A because its tool response was compacted away is a recovery failure.
pitfalls: Using the context window as the only database.
Summarizing untrusted content into trusted instructions.
Ignoring output and tool-response reserves.

question.prompt: Design a context and checkpoint strategy for a workflow that may be interrupted.
question.answer: Keep explicit durable state and stable operation identifiers outside the prompt. Retrieve evidence with provenance, preserve essential decisions during compaction, reserve output budget and revalidate stale facts. Reconstruct the next action from committed state and test repeated interruptions and retries against a deterministic environment.
followups: What counterexample would break your design?
What evidence would make you change this choice?
rubric: Reserve mandatory instructions and output budget.
Separate durable state from prompt context.
Preserve provenance through compaction.
Recover without repeating committed side effects.

title: Agent permissions, MCP and untrusted evidence
summary: Tool schemas describe capabilities; authorization must constrain which effects may actually occur.
explanation: A model proposing syntactically valid tool arguments has not established authorization. Enforce permissions in the execution layer, keep resource ownership and credential scopes explicit, and treat retrieved documents and tool output as untrusted evidence. For MCP integrations, examine confused-deputy risks, scope minimization and token handling. Combine approvals where needed with idempotency and durable audit state; prompting alone is not a security boundary.
example: A retrieved page tells an agent to upload a private file. The page can supply facts but cannot grant permission to disclose that file. A valid upload schema and a working token still do not authorize the requested effect.
pitfalls: Treating tool descriptions as grants of authority.
Passing upstream tokens through unchecked.
Assuming a prompt can replace server-side authorization.

question.prompt: How do you prevent a retrieved instruction from expanding an agent’s authority?
question.answer: Keep trusted user intent distinct from external content, validate resource-scoped authorization outside the model, minimize credentials, and restrict effects to an explicit policy. Test injected documents, confused-deputy scenarios, replay, and timeout-after-effect. Retain an audit trail that identifies which trusted intent authorized each operation.
followups: What counterexample would break your design?
What evidence would make you change this choice?
rubric: Separate user authority from retrieved evidence.
Enforce scope in the execution layer.
Discuss confused deputy and credential boundaries.
Test unauthorized effects and safe retry recovery.

title: Profiling before kernels or distributed training
summary: Identify the bottleneck and preserve correctness before changing execution strategy.
explanation: Measure representative steady-state steps with warmup and appropriate synchronization. Profile host data loading, transfers, operator shapes, allocation and device execution; a slow training step is not automatically a slow matrix multiplication. Inspect tensor layout, graph retention and compilation overhead. Only then consider checkpointing, compilation, a Triton kernel, or a distributed strategy. Multi-device scaling adds communication and state-partitioning costs that a single-device speedup cannot certify.
example: If a step waits on input for most of its duration, replacing an already-fast attention kernel may barely change throughput. Compare traces before and after one change with identical shapes, data and precision; keep correctness tolerances and peak memory in the report.
pitfalls: Timing asynchronous launches without synchronization.
Reporting only a compiled warm path without startup cost.
Scaling to more devices before locating a bottleneck.

question.prompt: How would you decide whether to optimize a kernel, the input pipeline or distributed execution?
question.answer: Capture a representative trace, separate warmup/compilation from steady-state work, and identify where time and memory go. Change one factor, check numerical behavior, then measure the same workload. For distributed work, account for collectives, global loss normalization and checkpoint state rather than assuming linear scaling.
followups: What counterexample would break your design?
What evidence would make you change this choice?
rubric: Profile representative inputs and actual device work.
Separate compile, input, compute and communication costs.
Preserve numerical and objective equivalence.
Report hardware, warmup, memory and repeat measurements.

title: Verifiable rewards and reasoning compute budgets
summary: A reward must detect real task success before it can safely guide reasoning optimization.
explanation: Reasoning systems can allocate additional inference work to candidates, checks or refinement. Compare quality under a fixed total budget, not merely per visible answer. Verifiable-reward training relies on a testable success criterion, but parsers, tests and reward implementations can be exploitable. Study GRPO objectives and failure modes after reliable SFT and evaluation; the browser exercise below is a prerequisite score calculation, not a GRPO implementation or a validated training run.
example: A program that prints a plausible answer can satisfy a weak string-based reward while failing the intended computation. Create hidden counterexamples, reject malformed outputs, and compare a verifier with independent ground truth before rewarding additional sampled attempts.
pitfalls: Optimizing an exploitable reward proxy.
Ignoring the total cost of multiple candidates.
Claiming GRPO quality from a scalar reward calculation.

question.prompt: What must be validated before using an automatic reward for reasoning optimization?
question.answer: Define task success, validate the verifier against independent ground truth and adversarial examples, and measure false acceptance as well as rejection. Hold out tasks and fix the total candidate/token budget when comparing strategies. Only then study or run an objective such as GRPO, with explicit attention to reward normalization and training/inference mismatch.
followups: What counterexample would break your design?
What evidence would make you change this choice?
rubric: Define success independently of fluent prose.
Test false accepts and reward exploits.
Hold out task families and fix total compute budget.
Separate verifier tests from actual optimization evidence.

title: Mixture-of-experts routing and expert parallelism
summary: Active parameters estimate token work; resident parameters and routing skew determine whether the experts can actually serve the batch.
explanation: A sparse MoE feed-forward block computes router scores, selects top-k routed experts, and combines their outputs with routing weights; shared experts, if present, run separately. Expert parallelism places different experts on different ranks. Dispatch sends token activations to their assigned ranks, then a return exchange combines results. A capacity-limited design can drop, reroute or delay excess assignments; make that policy explicit. Balancing losses or routing biases discourage persistent skew, but uniform average counts do not bound a rank’s tail load. The Meta/NVIDIA vLLM report is a system-specific engineering result: expert placement, dispatch precision and communication matter alongside expert GEMMs.
example: With 2B shared/dense weights, eight 1B experts and top-2 routing, the model has 10B resident and 4B active parameters per token. Ideal BF16 weights total 20 GB decimal before overhead or replication. For 1,024 tokens and four ranks, ideal load is 512 assignments per rank; a hot rank with 900 has 1.76× the mean. Examine per-rank send/receive bytes and compute time before buying more experts.
pitfalls: Sizing HBM from active parameters rather than all loaded experts.
Using mean expert load as a bound on rank tails.
Treating every dispatch byte as cross-node traffic or ignoring the combine exchange.

sources.title: Meta and NVIDIA: vLLM WideEP on Blackwell

question.prompt: An 8-expert, top-2 model has 2B dense/shared weights and 1B per expert. Why can it miss decode latency after adding expert-parallel ranks, and what do you measure first?
question.answer: Start with 10B resident vs 4B active parameters and 20 GB of ideal aggregate BF16 weights; account separately for replicated dense/shared weights, scales, KV and workspace. Measure assignment histograms, busiest-rank compute and both dispatch and combine on a per-layer timeline; classify intra-node versus cross-node bytes. A larger group can reduce per-rank weight memory but add synchronization, small GEMMs and cross-node traffic. Replay a fixed length/concurrency mix and compare p95 inter-token latency and goodput. Evaluate a placement or balancing change without silently changing capacity/drop policy or output quality.
followups: What changes if shared weights are replicated across four ranks?
How would you distinguish router skew from a slow fabric link?
rubric: Derives resident and active parameters separately.
Accounts for replication and runtime memory.
Identifies top-k dispatch, combine and rank-tail imbalance.
Proposes a controlled replay with quality and latency gates.

title: Multi-head Latent Attention and cache economics
summary: MLA compresses each token’s cached representation; temporal compression and sparse position selection are separate design choices.
explanation: In the DeepSeek-V2 MLA construction, a learned down-projection produces a shared KV latent. Head-specific up-projections recover key/value contributions; key projections can be absorbed into the query-side computation and value projections moved to the output-side computation, avoiding full KV reconstruction in the cache. The decoupled rotary key is cached separately so positions still affect scores. The formula compares ideal per-layer storage for equal dtype and a single copy of every logical cache element. DeepSeek-V4’s reported CSA/HCA additionally compresses over positions with different selection/coverage rules; do not reuse the V2 byte formula for that hybrid architecture.
equation: B_{\mathrm{GQA}}=L T b\,2h_{kv}d,\qquad B_{\mathrm{MLA}}=L T b(r+d_{\mathrm{rope}})
example: For 40 layers, 8,192 tokens, BF16, eight KV heads of width 128, GQA needs 1,280 MiB. A rank-512 latent and 64-wide rotary key need 360 MiB under the ideal single-copy model. Report 3.56× logical savings, then measure physical pages, sharding/replication, kernel bandwidth and decode latency. Do not infer equivalent model quality or 3.56× speed.
pitfalls: Omitting the separately cached positional key.
Equating a smaller logical cache with the same reduction in physical memory or latency.
Confusing latent width reduction with dropping or pooling earlier positions.

question.prompt: Budget the cache for 40 layers and 8,192 BF16 tokens using eight GQA KV heads of width 128 versus MLA with rank 512 and a rotary key of width 64. Which deployment conclusions follow?
question.answer: GQA stores 2,048 elements per token-layer and MLA stores 576, yielding 1,280 and 360 MiB respectively. Explain the learned shared latent, the separate rotary key, and why projection absorption can avoid materializing expanded K/V during decoding. A paged implementation may round capacity; tensor parallelism can shard one representation and replicate another. Pin model, workload, dtype and parallelism when measuring allocated cache, p95 decode latency and quality; the byte ratio alone gives none of those guarantees.
followups: When can a sharded GQA layout beat a replicated MLA layout in per-rank bytes?
What changes if a scheme also merges earlier token positions?
rubric: Computes both values with consistent units.
Includes the positional cache component.
Separates algebraic storage from physical allocation and kernel cost.
Distinguishes channel compression from sequence compression.

title: FSDP, ZeRO and the exposed communication path
summary: Sharding lowers persistent bytes per rank, but gathered parameters and unhidden collectives can dominate the peak and the step.
explanation: ZeRO stages progressively partition optimizer states, then gradients, then parameters across the data-parallel group. FSDP2 shards parameters and can all-gather a module before compute, then reduce-scatter gradients; resharding after forward saves residency at the cost of another gather for backward. Parameter all-gathers, activation retention, prefetch buffers, mixed dtypes and optimizer implementation determine peaks. Estimate payload by collective and group, then inspect the slowest rank’s GPU/network timeline: a collective of duration c overlapped by o only exposes max(0,c−o) on that dependency. Prefer topology-aware groups and tune wrap/prefetch granularity from evidence.
example: Assume 6B parameters, BF16 weights/gradients and two FP32 moments, no master copy, eight ranks. Fully sharded persistent state is 9 GB/rank decimal; add 3 GB/rank if the optimizer retains FP32 masters. A 25 ms gather with 18 ms of usable overlap exposes 7 ms in the toy timeline. Compare slowest-rank traces and peaks before moving the sharding group across hosts.
pitfalls: Treating persistent sharded state as peak memory.
Comparing aggregate link bandwidth with a serial critical path.
Changing global tokens per update when comparing microbatch settings.

sources.title: ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models

question.prompt: An eight-rank FSDP2 run fits in memory but slows down after adding a second host. How would you isolate and reduce exposed communication without changing the effective batch?
question.answer: Keep global non-padding tokens per update and precision fixed. Establish persistent and peak memory by rank and annotate forward/backward gathers, reduce-scatter, data waits and compute. Correlate collective tails with topology and stragglers; profiler timestamps reveal exposed work better than summing all collective durations. Test node-local sharding with cross-node replication/synchronization or adjust module wrapping and prefetch. Check memory, tokens/s, gradient parity and resumption under a known checkpoint before rolling out.
followups: What is traded away by keeping parameters materialized through backward?
How could sampler skew masquerade as network slowdown?
rubric: Explains the difference between ZeRO state partitions and FSDP collectives.
Separates transient peak from persistent state.
Measures the critical path and rank tails under a fixed workload.
Proposes a topology or scheduling intervention with parity checks.

title: Durable agent harnesses and crash recovery
summary: A context handoff preserves intent; a durable workflow checkpoint plus effect reconciliation preserves execution correctness.
explanation: Keep an authoritative workflow record with step identity, immutable input digest, authorization binding, tool attempt, receipt and verified completion. Save a pending record before the external call. A crash between the effect and the local commit creates an ambiguous state: recover with provider lookup or a provider-supported idempotency key, not by guessing from the model transcript. If neither is available, pause for reconciliation. Use fencing or a single writer when workers can overlap, and preserve the operation key across replans. Anthropic’s published harness uses progress artifacts across context windows; those are a handoff pattern, not an exactly-once protocol.
example: An invoice job dies after the gateway accepted a charge but before the receipt was written. On restart, consult the original operation key and receipt status. Replay only through a provider guarantee or verified no-effect result; if the provider reports unknown, halt. Inject crashes before the call, after the effect and after local commit, and assert the external charge count plus the final ledger state.
pitfalls: Treating a prose summary as a receipt.
Generating a fresh operation key on retry.
Promising exactly-once effects without a provider guarantee or an atomic transaction boundary.

sources.title: Anthropic: Effective harnesses for long-running agents

question.prompt: A workflow restarts after a tool times out during a consequential external write. Design the restart decision and a test that would catch duplicate effects.
question.answer: Persist intent, payload digest and operation key before acting. On resume reconcile authoritative receipts and reject a conflicting digest or revoked authority. If a matching effect is verified, commit locally with no repeat call. If verified absent, revalidate authority and retry with the original key under the documented consistency contract. If status is unknown, pause unless the provider guarantees deduplication. Fault-inject on either side of the external effect and local commit, with duplicate workers and delayed receipts; count actual external effects and check state, not just returned prose.
followups: What changes when a provider's lookup is eventually consistent?
How would you stop a previous worker from writing after a lease expires?
rubric: Identifies the ambiguous crash window.
Persists stable identity, digest and authorization before acting.
Separates absent, committed and unknown outcomes.
Tests the effect count under crash, retry and concurrency.

title: Budgeted agent evaluations and calibrated uncertainty
summary: Compare whole agent systems on representative tasks under matched budgets, with task-level uncertainty and separate reliability metrics.
explanation: Define a task distribution and a versioned, resettable environment with independent state-based graders. Freeze tool permissions, model/harness revisions, wall time, token/tool limits and retry policy. Repeat each configuration per task with reset state, report one-run success and safety failures, and pair comparisons on the same tasks. Resample task families or tasks as clusters rather than pretending correlated reruns are independent new tasks. Calibration concerns whether predicted success probabilities match outcomes; evaluate on held-out tasks with reliability bins and a proper score. METR’s time horizon uses human task duration as a difficulty proxy, not agent runtime or a reliability warranty. OpenAI’s November 2026 comparison found a safety evaluation could score below approximately matched deployment decisions. Select production-like cases before inspecting outcomes and report differences in tools, prompts and case mix; the direction and size of that study’s gap need not transfer.
example: On one task a harness passes 8/10 and another 9/10 within the same budget. That does not establish a general improvement. Compare task-wise deltas across a representative suite, bootstrap the sampled units, and report how often success comes with prohibited side effects. An operator may prefer more consistent repeated success to a higher best-of-many score.
pitfalls: Reporting pass-at-many against a one-attempt baseline.
Treating ten repeats of one task as ten independent tasks.
Dropping timeouts or labeling model confidence as calibrated without held-out evidence.

sources.title: Anthropic: Demystifying evals for AI agents
OpenAI: Eval-production behavior gaps in agent safety

question.prompt: Two harnesses report 70% and 76% on a task suite, but the second retries more and the tasks share templates. What experiment could support shipping the second?
question.answer: Reset state for every trial and pair harnesses on fixed task instances, versions and permissions. Report matched one-attempt budgets and separately an operational policy including retries at equal total budget. Count timeouts as failed and record safety violations, spend and latency separately. Predeclare target task weights and cluster the paired bootstrap by independent template family, preserving repeats within each cluster. Report intervals and tails, then validate on held-out task families; calibrate any abstention score on a split separate from routing-policy selection.
followups: What if the highest-impact tasks are too rare for a tight interval?
How would you report best-of-three without confusing it with all-three reliability?
rubric: Controls budget, retry policy and environment reset.
Defines outcome grading and tracks safety separately.
Uses paired cluster-level uncertainty rather than per-run pseudoreplication.
Separates calibration data and final held-out evidence.

title: Reward hacking and adversarial verifier evaluation
summary: An optimizer amplifies exploitable errors in a proxy, so validate the verifier under the policy that will optimize against it.
explanation: A deterministic checker can still be incomplete, and a learned reward model can prefer style over truth or fail out of distribution. Separate the scored proxy from an independent success oracle. Build challenge sets with equivalent correct outputs, convincing incorrect outputs, partial solutions and tampering attempts; measure false accepts and false rejects by slice. Keep grading assets and credentials outside the actor’s writable/reachable boundary. Sweep optimization pressure on frozen external evaluations and monitor divergence between proxy and audited outcomes. Anthropic’s 2026 reward-seeker experiment deliberately used vulnerable environments; its reported behaviors are evidence from that setting, not estimates for normal deployments.
example: A code agent’s proxy reward climbs from 0.70 to 0.90 while independently verified success drops from 0.68 to 0.60. Audit traces for skipped tests and grader exposure; check task-family mix and grader drift before attributing causality. Reject rollout until failure modes reproduce, the scorer boundary is hardened and untouched evaluation recovers.
pitfalls: Using a second prompt on the same biased judge as ground truth.
Reporting accuracy alone when false accepts are rare but costly.
Rewarding intermediate traces that the policy can fabricate rather than testing resulting state.

sources.title: Anthropic: Training a Misaligned Reward Seeker
Anthropic: Investigating unintended model actions in evaluations and internal use
OpenAI: How we detect frontier model misalignment

question.prompt: A training run improves the coding verifier score but regresses independent task success. How do you establish the failure mode and make the next training gate robust?
question.answer: Confirm that data, task weights and evaluator versions did not change. Sample disagreements and adjudicate final environment state using an independent oracle. Run positive controls with equivalent correct answers and negative controls that bypass tests or manipulate artifacts. Report conditional false accepts and false rejects, then isolate the grader and reserve untouched adversarial tasks. Sweep training pressure and compare proxy/audit curves and safety events at fixed sampling. Block promotion on predefined audited thresholds even when proxy reward improves.
followups: How can you estimate false accepts when you can afford only sparse human audits?
Why should some verifier attacks remain hidden from the training policy?
rubric: Separates policy optimization, proxy and independent oracle.
Tests both false accepts and false rejects by slice.
Restricts access to grading state and credentials.
Requires a predeclared rollout gate on untouched audit data.

title: Quantized serving under quality and latency constraints
summary: Choose a format per tensor and target kernel, then compare measured candidates under the same workload and quality gates.
explanation: Weight-only quantization compresses parameter reads while activations may stay high precision; W8A8 or W4A4 also changes the activation path, and cache quantization is separate. Group or block scales trade metadata for finer range fitting. Widening selected layers can protect sensitive distributions. A nominal four-bit format is not a throughput promise: packing, scales, layout, accumulator dtype, dequantization and available hardware kernels determine actual cost. PTQ calibrates or derives a quantization mapping from a trained checkpoint; QAT adapts training to the quantized forward approximation. Compare calibrated slices, actual allocated memory and long-context latency before selecting a format.
equation: M_{\mathrm{packed}}\approx P\,b/8 + N_{\mathrm{groups}}s,\qquad \min C \quad\text{s.t.}\quad Q_j\ge q_j,\ L_{95}\le \ell,\ M\le m
example: An INT4 weight-only candidate fits a smaller GPU but misses long-context p95 from fallback kernels; FP8 fits the original GPU and passes tail/quality targets. A mixed-precision variant passes average accuracy but drops rare-language quality below its floor. Among feasible candidates choose minimum measured cost per successful request, keeping revision, prompts and decoding fixed.
pitfalls: Picking by average quality while a critical slice regresses.
Comparing format labels without checking native versus fallback kernels.
Counting packed weights but omitting scales, cache, padding or workspace.

sources.title: Meta and NVIDIA: vLLM WideEP on Blackwell
DaoCloud: Serving GLM-5.2 with vLLM on B300 GPUs

question.prompt: Three checkpoint formats pass aggregate quality; one fails a long-context latency objective, one fails a rare-language quality floor, and one meets both at higher GPU-hour cost. How do you decide and what data do you demand?
question.answer: Use the service and quality thresholds as gates, not weights that average away a failure. Pin workload mix, runtime version, hardware, calibration and decoder; validate slice quality with uncertainty, report TTFT and inter-token tails, and inspect the real kernel path and memory breakdown. Select among feasible formats by end-to-end cost per successful in-SLO request including replica count and utilization. If none pass, test selectively higher precision and rerun the same gates. A measured win on a reported Blackwell deployment is a candidate, not a result for our workload.
followups: How would you isolate whether the failure comes from KV-cache or weight quantization?
How do changes in batch size alter the winner even on identical hardware?
rubric: Separates weight, activation and cache precision.
Enforces slice-specific quality and service constraints.
Verifies runtime/kernel support and measured memory.
Uses cost per useful request instead of nominal bit width or GPU price.

title: Multimodal tokenization and grounded evaluation
summary: A fluent answer can be visually wrong; test whether changing the evidence changes the answer for the right reason.
explanation: A vision encoder converts patches or regions into representations, and a projector or adapter connects them to the language model. Some systems fuse text and vision tokens in one sequence, others cross-attend to a separate visual stream. Patch size, resizing and pooling control token count and small-object recall; video sampling adds a temporal bottleneck. Grounding is the ability to tie a claim to the right region, frame or source, not merely to describe plausible content. Qwen’s released Qwen3.5 model card describes native early fusion; it does not imply that all multimodal architectures use that design or support reliable grounding.
example: A 1,024×1,024 image with 16-pixel patches yields 4,096 patches before merging or downsampling. A chart assistant gives the same trend when labels are swapped. Compare text-only and shuffled-image controls, high-resolution crops, and counterfactual charts. Score both answer correctness and whether the cited region contains the relevant datum; use IoU only when region annotation fits the task.
pitfalls: Equating verbal fluency or OCR accuracy with grounded reasoning.
Comparing pixel counts without tracking resizing and visual token budgets.
Using only easy images whose labels can be guessed from accompanying text.

sources.title: Alibaba: Qwen3.5 release and native multimodality

question.prompt: A vision-language model answers dashboard questions well in aggregate but misses small units and seems unchanged by swapped plots. Design a grounding evaluation and one model-side experiment.
question.answer: Build matched chart pairs with altered axes, labels and traces and hold their templates out of tuning. Score answer changes, region localization where annotatable, and calibrated abstention; include text-only and image-shuffled controls. Slice by font size, resolution and plot family. Trace resizing, patching and pooling; test a crop or higher-resolution tiling at fixed total serving budget. Report improvement on the small-unit slice and any latency or hallucination regressions rather than a single accuracy number.
followups: How would you score an answer supported by two disjoint regions?
How would you separate temporal sampling failures from reasoning on the sampled frames?
rubric: Explains visual token and resolution tradeoffs.
Uses counterfactual evidence and no-image controls.
Scores localization separately from final answers.
Compares slice improvements under a realistic resource budget.

title: Synthetic data lineage and contamination prevention
summary: Data quality needs provenance, family-aware splits, held-out evaluation and audits of both near-duplicate and generated examples.
explanation: Record source, license or consent basis, capture time, stable content fingerprint, transformation chain, and teacher version and prompt lineage for generated material. Deduplicate exact copies and build candidate near-duplicate clusters using shingles or embeddings with measured false-match rates. Split by connected source/template family before generation, then quarantine suspect overlap against held-out benchmarks. Hash equality will miss paraphrases and translated solutions. Preserve diverse verified human data, audit synthetic correctness and coverage, and run mixture ablations under fixed tokens and untouched evaluations. FineWeb2 documents language-aware filtering and deduplication; results from individual contamination studies do not prove a universal overlap detector.
example: A generated tutoring corpus passes exact dedup but contains translated solutions from held-out tasks. Move the source families and synthetic descendants into quarantine, audit candidate semantic matches in multiple languages, and report contamination decisions with threshold and reviewer precision. Rerun equal-token mixture ablations on a new frozen set with hard negative and rare-domain slices.
pitfalls: Splitting documents after paraphrasing instead of before family expansion.
Using a similarity threshold as proof that no leakage remains.
Counting more synthetic examples without auditing correlated errors, diversity or provenance.

sources.title: Soft Contamination Means Benchmarks Test Shallow Generalization

question.prompt: A synthetic training expansion raises held-out benchmark scores, but you discover that the teacher prompts and benchmarks share source documents. What can you still claim, and how do you rebuild the experiment?
question.answer: Treat affected scores as contaminated evidence, not as generalization. Recover source identifiers and generation lineage; split connected source/template families before synthesis. Search for exact, lexical and semantic overlap with sampled adjudication, including translations and cross-hop relations. Build a fresh frozen holdout inaccessible to the generation loop. Compare human-only and mixed runs at matched token budgets and versions; measure grounded correctness, rare domains and audit yield, and record what your scanner cannot detect.
followups: How do you handle a chain of near duplicates spanning both splits?
What if the upstream teacher’s own training mixture is unknown?
rubric: Identifies leakage beyond exact string matches.
Propagates family membership through transformations.
Separates detection uncertainty from the final held-out estimate.
Uses a controlled mixture ablation and documents provenance limits.

title: Serving goodput, disaggregation and unit economics
summary: Measure useful completions within an SLO, not just generated tokens or peak throughput.
explanation: Measure time to first token from arrival (queue plus processing and transport) and inter-token latency from streamed gaps; document whether TPOT averages generation time per request. Prefill tends to have more parallel work, while decode repeatedly reads model and cache state; the bottleneck depends on batching, hardware and model. Separating prefill and decode lets each pool scale and tune independently but adds KV transfer, network contention and two admission queues. Count correct non-cancelled completions meeting declared thresholds over observation time and charge all reserved GPU time, including idle periods and failed attempts. A vLLM case study reports a deployed topology and its own SLA metrics, not universal gains.
example: In a 30-minute replay, eight GPUs at $3 per GPU-hour cost $12. If 6,000 of 10,000 arrivals meet both service and quality gates, goodput is 3.33 requests/s and GPU-only cost is $0.002 per eligible request. A transfer-heavy topology may boost tokens/s while lowering this goodput. Test warm and cold starts and length/concurrency mixes separately.
pitfalls: Reporting GPU-only service time as client-visible latency.
Ignoring retries, idle allocation and requests that timed out before any token.
Averaging tails across request classes or comparing reports with different SLO definitions.

sources.title: DaoCloud: Serving GLM-5.2 with vLLM on B300 GPUs
Meta and NVIDIA: vLLM WideEP on Blackwell

question.prompt: Disaggregating prefill and decode improves peak tokens/s by 20% but raises p95 first-token latency. How would you decide whether to ship under a fixed monthly GPU budget?
question.answer: Replay the same arrival process and length mix, including bursts, with equal hardware cost envelopes. Instrument ingress queue, prefix hits, prefill, transfer bandwidth and queueing, decode gaps and cancellations. Use explicit per-request SLOs and quality gates, then report goodput, cost per eligible completion, latency tails and capacity with uncertainty. Inspect pool imbalance and network contention; tune ratios or bypass remote prefill for small requests. Ship only if the target mix improves without breaking protected tail and quality thresholds.
followups: What happens to cost if a prefill pool sits idle while decode is saturated?
How do you test transfer bottlenecks without confounding changes in prefix cache hits?
rubric: Defines client-visible latency and eligible-request denominator.
Accounts for all allocated GPU time and failures.
Tests the topology under fixed budget and representative arrivals.
Identifies KV transfer and pool imbalance as measurable costs.

title: Computer-use agents and delegated permissions
summary: Pixels, DOM text and accessibility labels describe a UI; only the host can grant authority to act on it.
explanation: Treat visual or semantic observations as untrusted inputs. Bind delegated authority to principal, destination, resource, action, parameters, expiry and a one-time operation where appropriate. The host must check action proposals before execution, including the resolved origin and data crossing the boundary. Use an isolated browser profile with scoped accounts and restricted file/network access. For consequential actions, show the user the exact effect and revalidate after confirmation: a stale button or redirected page can change the target. Product system cards and OpenAI’s prompt-injection reports illustrate specific defenses and observed behaviors; model classifiers and UI labels cannot guarantee policy enforcement.
example: A user delegates drafting a refund on a merchant site. A fake modal in a support ticket asks the agent to upload customer data and click submit. A host policy permits draft edits only, rejects the upload target, and requires a fresh user confirmation bound to exact refund amount and order ID for submission. Test with pop-ups, renamed controls, redirects and delayed UI transitions.
pitfalls: Assuming screenshot or DOM instructions inherit user authority.
Treating approval for a draft or for one order as blanket approval.
Checking the visible label but failing to bind the effective target or upload data.

question.prompt: An agent may draft a refund in a browser. The page asks it to export customer records and the refund button’s target changes after confirmation. What must the host enforce and how do you test it?
question.answer: Keep task authority separate from UI observations. Give the agent only the session and destination it needs; deny exports and unapproved writes at the host or restrict capabilities if a click cannot be classified reliably. Confirm consequential effects with exact resource, destination and parameters, bind consent to that state and expire it on mutation or navigation. Validate the resolved destination and payload immediately before acting and audit actual effects. Test malicious visible text, DOM injection, redirect and stale-approval cases with a trusted side-effect oracle, including benign requests to detect overblocking.
followups: What if all interactions are coordinate clicks and the host cannot classify a transition?
How do you prevent an attack from propagating via a seemingly authorized draft?
rubric: Separates authority from observation channels.
Limits data, account and action scope outside the model.
Binds approval to effective destination and current parameters.
Tests real effects, stale consent and benign cases.

title: Adaptive test-time compute and stopping policies
summary: Spend additional reasoning only when it improves expected utility enough to justify latency, cost and risk.
explanation: Test-time scaling may allocate extra tokens, independent samples, verifier-guided search or a stronger model. A router chooses how much to spend before or during execution; a stopping rule uses a held-out calibrated decision signal, bounded by hard time, token and tool budgets. Simple independent sampling gives the displayed pass-at-k expression for finding at least one correct candidate, but outputs are correlated and picking the correct one requires a selector. Optimize expected gain net of resource and risk costs; count escalations, retries, abandoned attempts and queueing in end-to-end comparisons. DeepMind’s published compute-allocation research and Google’s Deep Think release are different kinds of evidence, neither a recipe for private routing logic.
equation: P(\text{at least one success})=1-(1-p)^k,\qquad \mathrm{continue\ if}\ \mathbb E[\Delta U\mid s]>\lambda\,\Delta C
example: A cheap model solves short factual tasks reliably but its confidence is poorly calibrated on proofs. Use cheap routing for verified easy tasks, escalate borderline ones to a stronger model or verifier, and stop when a reliable check passes or the remaining SLA budget cannot cover another attempt. Compare to cheap-only and strong-only at matched cost or latency and track difficult-slice abstention.
pitfalls: Treating independent pass-at-k as selected-answer accuracy.
Training the stopping policy and reporting its quality on the same examples.
Ignoring extra attempts’ queueing, verification overhead and correlated failure modes.

sources.title: Snell et al.: Scaling LLM test-time compute optimally
Google Deep Think team: Gemini 3 Deep Think update

question.prompt: You can either sample a cheap model three times or escalate once to a stronger model. Design a policy that meets a 2-second tail budget and a quality floor on hard tasks.
question.answer: Define utility, deadlines and policy budget up front. Measure cost and quality by difficulty and judge reliability; keep the strongest model as a baseline. Use held-out calibrated expected gain to choose another sample or escalation and reserve time for verification. Stop on verified success, low marginal gain or deadline, otherwise abstain or hand off. Compare fixed routes and the adaptive policy on paired unseen tasks under equal cost or latency, include queueing and cancellations, and report selector errors, hard-slice quality and abstention coverage.
followups: If three samples share a common misconception, what changes in your gain estimate?
How would you adapt when the verification signal shifts after a model upgrade?
rubric: Chooses an explicit stopping signal and hard resource caps.
Separates candidate availability from selector success.
Calibrates on data separate from evaluation.
Measures matched cost, quality slices and deadline failures.
